title: L9 · Spine & Thoracic Cage
subtitle: Vertebrae, regional features, spinal curves, ribs, sternum

lines.text: The spine has 26 vertebrae. The top 24 move.
**Cervical**: 7, in the neck.
**Thoracic**: 12, in the upper back.
**Lumbar**: 5, in the low back.
The **sacrum** is 5 fused vertebrae. The **coccyx** is 4 fused.
Breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5.
The **body** is the big front part. It's largest in the lumbar spine.
Two **pedicles** project back from the body.
Two **laminae** meet in the midline.
Together they form the **spinous process**, the bump you feel down the back.
Superior **articular processes** meet the vertebra above.
Inferior articular processes meet the vertebra below.
**Transverse processes** project to the sides.
The **vertebral foramen** is the hole for the spinal cord.
Discs sit between the vertebrae.
They are **fibrocartilage**, the cartilage that resists compression.
They bear weight.
Cervical spinous processes are **bifid**, split in two.
They have two **transverse foramina**. The vertebral arteries run through them.
Their bodies are small. Their foramen is triangular.
The **atlas** is C1. It's a ring with no body and no spinous process.
It meets the occipital condyles.
The **axis** is C2.
Its **dens**, or odontoid process, points up into the atlas.
Only thoracic vertebrae have **rib facets**.
Their foramen is round. Their spinous processes point down.
Lumbar vertebrae have large bodies and a triangular foramen.
Their spinous process is wide and **spatulated**.
The sacrum is one triangle made of five fused vertebrae.
The **median sacral crest** is what's left of the spinous processes.
It has four pairs of **sacral foramina**.
The **coccyx** is the tailbone at its tip.
From behind, the spine should be straight. A sideways curve is **scoliosis**.
From the side, it curves.
**Lordosis** is in the cervical and lumbar spine. It's a secondary curve, formed after birth.
**Kyphosis** is in the thoracic and sacral spine. It's a primary curve, there from birth.
There are 12 pairs of ribs.
**True ribs** are 1 to 7. Their cartilage joins the sternum directly.
**False ribs** are 8 to 12. Their cartilage joins rib 7's, or nothing.
**Floating ribs** are 11 and 12. They have no cartilage.
The **head** meets the vertebral body.
The **neck** is between the head and the tubercle.
The **tubercle** meets the transverse process.
The body is the main part. The **angle** is where it curves forward.
The **manubrium** is on top. Rib 1 joins it. The jugular notch is at its top.
The **sternal angle**, or angle of Louis, is where rib 2 attaches.
The **body** is the largest part. Ribs 3 to 7 join it.
The **xiphoid** process is at the bottom. No ribs attach.
